canonicalExplanation.summary: A Git **repository** has two parts. The hidden **.git folder** is the database: every saved snapshot (**commit**), plus names like branches that point at commits. The **working tree** is the ordinary files you see and edit, one checked-out snapshot plus whatever you've changed since. Editing a file changes **only the working tree**; the saved commits don't change until you **stage** and **commit** new content. And not everything in the folder is versioned: new files are **untracked** until you add them, so generated files and secrets should never be added in the first place.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner creates a repository for their study notes, makes a first commit, then edits README.md. A friend asks: "Did that edit change your saved version?" The learner isn't sure whether Git saves everything in the folder automatically. Editing README changes the working tree but does not alter the last commit object until new content is staged and committed. In this lesson you'll initialize and inspect a repository without committing generated or secret files.

```predict
{"question": "You run `git init` in a folder with 10 files. How many are versioned now?", "options": ["All 10", "None yet: they're untracked until you add and commit them"], "answer": 1, "why": "git init creates the .git database; it doesn't save any files."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know the **Filesystem and terminal fluency** module and **List, read and search** (ls -la and git status).

sections.heading: The model: a database of snapshots plus a working copy
sections.body:
```bash
mkdir study-notes && cd study-notes
git init                          # creates the hidden .git database.
ls -la                            # shows .git/ next to your files.

echo "# Study notes" > README.md
git status                        # README.md is untracked.
git add README.md
git commit -m "Add README"        # first snapshot saved in .git.

echo "Week 1: loops" >> README.md
git status                        # modified in the working tree only.
git diff                          # the change vs the saved snapshot.
git show HEAD:README.md           # the committed version is unchanged.
```

| Part | What it is | Changed by |
|---|---|---|
| .git folder. | commits, branches, history. | git add, git commit, git fetch... |
| working tree. | files you see and edit. | your editor and shell commands. |
| untracked files. | in the folder, not in Git. | nothing until you git add them. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "What happens if you delete the .git folder?", "answer": "Your files stay, but all history, branches and commits are gone: the folder is no longer a repository. Never delete .git to \"reset\" something."}
```

sections.heading: Keep junk and secrets out

examples.title: Editing the README after the first commit
examples.situation: Editing README changes the working tree but does not alter the last commit object until new content is staged and committed.
walkthrough: **First commit:** git add README.md and git commit save the snapshot in .git.
**Edit changes the working tree:** appending "Week 1: loops" makes git status report README.md as modified.
**Inspect:** git diff shows the new line, while `git show HEAD:README.md` will print the old committed text, proving the commit didn't change.
examples.result: The learner knows the saved version is safe, and that a new commit is needed to record the edit.

examples.title: The first commit that included everything
examples.situation: A learner runs `git init`, then `git add .` and `git commit` in a web project. The commit includes 40,000 files from node_modules and an .env with an API key.
walkthrough: git add . stages every untracked file that isn't ignored.
Generated folders and secrets were never excluded.
Before the first add: create .gitignore, then check git status lists only source files.
examples.result: The first commit contains just the project's own files, with no secrets or generated output.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: The repository is just the visible project folder, so every file in it is automatically versioned.
misconceptions.correction: Git stores history in the hidden .git database, and only content you add and commit is versioned. Files in the folder stay untracked until added, and edits aren't saved until committed.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, how many files were versioned after git init?

analogy.example: A repository is like **a photo album plus the room you're photographing**. The room (working tree) changes all the time as you move things. The album (.git) only changes when you take and paste in a new photo (commit). Things you never photograph (untracked files) aren't in the album at all.
limitations: Photos can't be edited; commits can't either, only replaced by new ones.
Throwing away the album (deleting .git) loses every past photo.

artifact: git status / git diff / git show HEAD:README.md

trace.textAlternative: Tracing working tree vs commit. Step 1, Commit: HEAD is Add README; working tree is same as commit. The first snapshot is saved in .git. Step 2, Edit: working tree is README modified; HEAD is unchanged. Editing README changes the working tree but does not alter the last commit object. Step 3, Inspect: git diff is +Week 1: loops; HEAD version is old text. Nothing is saved until new content is staged and committed.

nearTransfer.prompt: In a disposable folder, run git init, create two files, commit one of them, then edit it. Predict and then check what git status shows for each file.
expectedEvidence: git show HEAD:<file> prints the old version.

farTransfer.prompt: Initialise a repository for an existing small project that has a build folder and a .env file. Write a .gitignore first, check git status, make the first commit, and show with git ls-files that neither the build output nor .env is tracked.
expectedEvidence: A short note explaining each ignored entry.

remediation.explanation: Ask two questions: **Is this change in the working tree only, or committed?** (git status and git diff tell you.) **Is this file tracked at all?** (git ls-files tells you.)
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The first commit that included everything".

recap.summary: To initialize and inspect a repository, run git init to create the .git database, remember the working tree is just your editable files, that new files stay untracked until added and edits don't change any commit until staged and committed, and exclude generated and secret files before the first add.
